items.title: Annulus: which circle is removed?
items.student: Two concentric circles have outer radius 7 cm and inner radius 4 cm. The shaded ring is the annulus. Sketch the region, estimate its area and calculate it exactly in terms ofπ. Explain whyπ(7−4)² is not the area. Diagnostic: find a circle’s area when radius 3 cm, a right triangle’s area with perpendicular legs 6 cm and 8 cm, and distinguish a radius from a diameter. Diagram dimensions govern; do not measure the print.
items.teacher: Annulus areaπ(7²−4²)=33π cm²≈103.673 cm².π(7−4)²=9π wrongly treats ring thickness as a circle radius. Diagnostic 9π cm² and 24 cm²; diameter twice radius. Both radii have the same centre. Compare with the whole 49π cm² disk and removed 16π cm² disk. Useπ calculator value throughout unless exact form requested; round final approximations to 3 decimal places.

items.title: Annulus applications and inverse reasoning
items.student: Illustrative designs: (A) A circular path has outer diameter 10 m and inner diameter 6 m. Find its area. (B) A ring has outer radius 13 cm and area 25π cm²; find its inner radius and thickness. State a check and a modelling assumption in each case. (C) A learner calls a 3 m-wide path around a radius 4 m disk an annulus of radii 4 m and 3 m. Correct the dimensions before calculating.
items.teacher: A radii 5 m and 3 m; area 16π m²≈50.265 m². B inner radius√(169−25)=12 cm; thickness 1 cm; substituteπ(169−144)=25π. C outer radius 7 m, inner 4 m; area 33π m². Model assumes circular concentric boundaries and horizontal planar area; circumference/volume cannot substitute for area.

items.title: Sector as a fraction of a disk
items.student: A minor sector has radius 6 cm and central angle 120°. Relate its area to a whole disk. Calculate exact and approximate area. Then compare two sectors each with central angle 60° but radii 3 cm and 6 cm. Does doubling radius double area? State the central-angle fraction for 90°,180° and 360°. Label any sketch; the angle is measured at the centre.
items.teacher: Area(120/360)π6²=12π cm²≈37.699 cm². Radius 3,60° area 1.5π; radius 6,60° area 6π, a factor 4. Fractions 1/4,1/2,1. General sector area(θ/360)πr² forθ in degrees. The formula counts planar area; arc length uses a different expression. Derive the proportional relationship rather than relying on the drawing size.

items.title: Sector decisions and unknown angles
items.student: A circular planting design of radius 12 m allocates a 75° sector to flowers. Find the flower area. A second sector in the same disk has area 24π m²: find its angle. A supplier mistakenly uses the flower arc length as the soil-cover area. Explain the unit error. Assume boundaries are planar and measurements exact; no real purchasing price is supplied.
items.teacher: 75/360×π144=30π m²≈94.248 m².24π/(144π)×360=60°. Arc length is measured in metres whereas area is in square metres. Area results support a quantity estimate only; costs require an applicable price and real allowance/measurement checks.

items.title: Annular sector: subtract sectors with the same angle
items.student: Concentric circles have radii 10 cm and 6 cm. The ring portion spans 72° at their common centre. Sketch what is included and removed, then calculate its exact area. Compare (θ/360)π(R²−r²) with (θ/360)π(R−r)². Explain which expression is appropriate. Find the area if only the angle doubles to 144°.
items.teacher: Area 72/360×π(100−36)=64π/5=12.8π cm²≈40.212 cm². Incorrect thickness-squared expression gives 3.2π. Doubling only the angle gives 25.6π cm². Both circular sectors must share the centre, bounding rays and angle. If their angles or centres differ this subtraction cannot be used without reanalysing the region.

items.title: Minor segment: sector minus triangle
items.student: A chord AB joins two radii of length 8 cm making 90° at O. Shade the minor segment between the chord and minor arc AB. Find sector AOB area and triangle AOB area, then the minor segment. Explain why subtracting the triangle is required. Extension: calculate chord AB length using Pythagoras; do not confuse it with the arc.
items.teacher: Sector 16π cm²; right triangle(1/2)8×8=32 cm²; segment 16π−32≈18.265 cm². It is positive and smaller than the quarter disk. Chord 8√2 cm; arc is 4π cm, different. The diagram highlights the curved region beyond the chord, not the triangular wedge. Diagnose circle/triangle and square-unit prerequisites before proceeding.

items.title: Other angles and major segments
items.student: A circle has radius 10 cm. Chord AB subtends 60° at the centre. Draw the two segments. Find the minor segment from sector minus triangle, using triangle area(1/2)r²sinθ (degrees) or an equilateral-triangle height. Then find the major segment by subtracting the minor segment from the full disk. State why “major sector minus triangle” is not the major-segment formula for this drawing. Use exact√3/2 forsin 60° where possible.
items.teacher: Sector 50π/3 cm²; triangle 25√3 cm². Minor 50π/3−25√3≈9.059 cm². Major 100π−minor=250π/3+25√3≈305.101 cm². The major segment contains the major sector AND the triangle. For equilateral OAB, height 5√3 gives area 25√3. If trigonometry is not secure, use the supplied equilateral derivation; the diagnostic/support route must be recorded rather than assume missing Core 2.4 source requirements.

items.title: Common area of equal intersecting circles
items.student: Two circles each have radius 5 cm. Centres O1,O2 are 5√2 cm apart. The common chord PQ subtends 90° at each centre. The overlap is the region inside both disks, bounded by the two minor arcs PQ. Explain why it comprises two minor segments; calculate its area exactly and approximately. Use labelled radii/angles, not measurement from the print. Check that the result is smaller than either disk.
items.teacher: Each segment(90/360)π25−(1/2)25 sin 90°=25π/4−25/2. Overlap 2 segments=25π/2−25≈14.270 cm². Each right isosceles central triangle area 12.5 cm². A whole-circle sum double-counts the common region and does not isolate it. Symmetry justifies doubling here; that step does not hold automatically for unequal radii.

items.title: Common area when the circles differ
items.student: Circles have radii 3 cm about O1 and 4 cm about O2, centre distance 5 cm, intersections P and Q. The triangles O1 PO2 and O1 QO2 are right at P and Q. Central overlap-sector angles:θ1=2 tan⁻¹(4/3)≈106.260205° andθ2=2 tan⁻¹(3/4)≈73.739795°. Here tan⁻¹ means inverse tangent in degrees, not reciprocal tangent. Compute each sector area and each central triangle area(1/2)r²sinθ, then add the two segment areas. Explain why equal-circle doubling is inappropriate. Keep full calculator precision until the final answer.
items.teacher: Overlap[θ1/360×π9−4.32]+[θ2/360×π16−7.68]≈6.642 cm². The two central triangle areas total 12 cm²; equivalently subtract the kite made of two 3–4–5 right triangles, each area 6. Sector sum≈18.642 cm². Intermediate areas need not be equal. Use degree mode and full inverse-tangent values; given displayed angles yield the same 3-decimal result. The intersection geometry supplies enough data; never invent missing angles from a sketch.

items.title: Make and explain a safe circular design
items.student: Group paper project with individual evidence. Design a paper target or necklace ornament using concentric circles outer radius 12 cm, inner 8 cm, divided into eight equal annular sectors. No darts, throwing, blades or sharp improvised tools. Make a labelled paper model or accurate diagram; find each annular-sector area and total ring area. Explain one use of part-circle area, one material-saving or waste implication and one limitation of treating a real object as a planar design. Each learner supplies a separate calculation and explanation; groups may choose decorative colours. Adult-supervised scissors only if permitted; otherwise use pre-cut paper. Optional family discussion may supply ideas, but marks do not depend on home materials or family help. For full-size work the outer diameter is 24 cm, so use larger or joined paper. Alternatively draw at 1:2 linear scale with radii 6 cm and 4 cm, label the scale, and calculate the intended design area using the original 12 cm and 8 cm radii.
items.teacher: Each angle 45°. Ringπ(144−64)=80π cm²; each 10π cm²≈31.416 cm². Eight sectors reconstruct the ring; a diameter 24 cm outer circle supports the model. Award geometric reasoning independently of decoration. Prepare recovered clean paper, a compass, protractor and ruler, or teacher-prepared cut pieces; no downloadable project template is promised. A full-size outer diameter of 24 cm needs larger/joined paper. The 1:2 alternative uses drawing radii 6/4 cm while the stated design remains 12/8 cm; clearly label which dimensions enter the area calculation. Offer an accessible diagram route. Record contribution/collaboration and individual reasoning separately. A ring-area estimate ignores cutting waste, thickness and joining allowance; a real manufacturing estimate needs those data.

items.title: Select, critique and justify an area model
items.student: Audit these claims: A a ring of radii 9 cm and 5 cm has area 16π cm²; B a 90° sector of radius 4 cm has area 4π cm²; C a 90° minor segment of radius 4 cm has area 4π−8 cm²; D the overlap of any two circles is twice one of its segments. Correct false claims and identify information missing from D. Then choose one local circular object or use a drawn example; state dimensions/assumptions needed to estimate a part-circle area. Identify the region, formula/decomposition, units, check and limits. Do not measure risky machinery, roads or live equipment.
items.teacher: A false:π(81−25)=56π cm²; thickness 4 does not give a radius 4 disk. B and C correct; sector 4π and triangle 8. D only justified when the two relevant segment areas are equal, as in the symmetric equal-circle case; unequal radii generally require separate sector/triangle calculations and sufficient intersection geometry. Local example may be a paper decorative ring, garden sector or safe drawn windshield model; the swept wiper region needs both radii/angle and an appropriate annular-sector assumption. Do not claim a physically measured skill from a drawn case.

items.title: Independent part-circle geometry data
items.student: Useπ calculator value for approximations; exact expressions inπ and√3 are welcome. Dimensions are exact, drawings are schematic. A annulus: outer radius 8 cm, inner radius 5 cm. B minor sector: radius 9 cm, angle 80°. C annular sector: outer radius 9 cm, inner 6 cm, angle 80°. D minor segment: radius 10 cm, angle 90°. E two equal circles: each radius 6 cm; centres 6√3 cm apart; common chord PQ subtends 60° at each centre; overlap is bounded by the two minor arcs PQ. For E, sin 60°=√3/2. Formula support: circleπr²; sector(θ/360)πr²; triangle with two sides r,r and included angleθ has area(1/2)r²sinθ. Explain your decomposition; using a provided formula alone is not a full explanation.
items.teacher: Keep isolated until Lesson 12. A39π; B18π; C10π; D25π−50; E12π−18√3, all cm². The equal-circle overlap contains two congruent minor segments, each 6π−9√3. This sheet intentionally supplies geometry/formula information but no worked area answer. The separate key/rubric carries exemplars.
